scenarios.title: Soft landing
scenarios.story: Inflation drifts back toward the Fed's 2% goal without many people losing their jobs. The Fed can cut rates slowly, borrowing gets cheaper, and company profits keep growing.
chain: The Fed can lower interest rates without fearing a rebound in prices
Lower rates make borrowing cheaper and future profits worth more today
Stocks broaden out: smaller and debt-heavy companies benefit most

industries.how: More lending, but a smaller gap between what they pay and earn on deposits.

industries.name: Cash & money funds
industries.how: Interest on savings falls with the Fed's rate.

scenarios.title: Running hot
scenarios.story: The economy stays strong enough that prices start rising faster again. Instead of cutting, the Fed holds rates high or raises them. Profits grow, but the rates used to value them rise too.
chain: Strong demand and tight hiring push wages and prices up
The Fed keeps rates high - or raises them
Bond yields rise, so future profits are worth less today
Companies with profits now beat companies promising profits later

scenarios.title: Stagflation
scenarios.story: The economy weakens but prices keep rising - often because of an energy or supply shock. The Fed is stuck: cutting rates would feed inflation, holding them hurts jobs. Stocks and bonds can fall together.
chain: A cost shock (oil, tariffs, wages) keeps prices rising
Households' money buys less, so they spend less
The Fed can't cut to help, because inflation is still high
Profits shrink while borrowing stays expensive - the worst mix for stocks and bonds

scenarios.title: Downturn
scenarios.story: Hiring stops and layoffs rise. Inflation falls with demand, so the Fed cuts rates quickly - but company profits fall first, and stocks usually drop before the cuts help.

People spend less, so company sales and profits fall
Inflation drops, so the Fed cuts rates fast
Bonds rise; stocks fall first and recover once the cuts work

active.title: Oil gets expensive
active.first: Petrol, jet fuel, diesel and plastics cost more within weeks.
active.second: Airlines, truckers and chemical makers see margins squeezed; households spend more on fuel and less on everything else. Inflation readings rise, so the Fed is slower to cut.
active.long_run: Sustained high prices pay for new drilling (more supply later) and speed the shift to EVs, efficiency and renewables - which is why oil spikes tend to undo themselves over 1-2 years.

industries.name: Oil & gas producers
industries.how: Selling price rises; costs mostly don't.

industries.name: Oilfield services
industries.how: Producers drill more when prices stay high.

industries.name: Airlines
industries.how: Fuel is ~25% of their costs.

industries.name: Trucking & delivery
industries.how: Diesel costs, passed on only with a lag.

industries.name: Chemicals & plastics
industries.how: Oil is both feedstock and energy.

industries.name: Retail & restaurants
industries.how: Customers have less left after filling the tank.

active.breaks_if: Prices fall back quickly (OPEC adds supply, demand weakens), or the economy is strong enough to absorb them.
test: Headline inflation higher in three months
why_now: Oil is up 26% in three months ($102 a barrel).
5 recent headlines, e.g. "Brent oil touches $110 as Iran escalates Hormuz attacks, Ukraine vows to hit Russian refineries"

active.title: Rates stay high for longer
active.first: Mortgages, car loans, credit cards and company loans stay expensive.
active.second: Housing sales freeze (owners won't give up cheap old mortgages); companies that must refinance debt pay much more; profits expected far in the future are worth less today, so high-valuation stocks fall most.
active.long_run: A 'refinancing wall' as cheap pandemic-era debt matures: weaker borrowers default, banks holding commercial-property loans take losses. Savers and insurers earn more.

industries.name: Banks & insurers
industries.how: Earn more on loans and on the bonds they hold.

industries.name: Money-market funds
industries.how: Cash pays 4-5% with no risk.

industries.name: Homebuilders & real estate
industries.how: Buyers can't afford the monthly payment.

industries.how: Floating-rate debt costs rise directly.

industries.name: Unprofitable tech
industries.how: Valued on distant profits, discounted at a higher rate.

industries.name: Regional banks
industries.how: Office and property loans go bad; old low-rate bonds lose value.

active.breaks_if: Inflation drops clearly and the Fed signals cuts, or something breaks in credit and forces cuts.
test: Home sales lower in three months
why_now: The 10-year Treasury yield is 5.10%, and the Fed's stance reads as restrictive.

active.title: The AI spending boom
active.first: Big tech companies spend hundreds of billions a year on data centres and chips.
active.second: Chipmakers, memory makers and network gear sellers book record sales; data centres need huge amounts of power, so utilities, grid equipment, cooling and copper demand rise; software companies worry AI tools replace their products.
active.long_run: Either AI earns back the spending - productivity rises across the economy - or spending gets cut, and the suppliers who grew fastest fall hardest. Electricity prices for everyone may rise either way.

industries.name: Semiconductors & memory
industries.how: Direct sellers of the chips.

industries.name: Utilities & grid equipment
industries.how: Data centres need new power plants and lines.

industries.name: Copper & electrical
industries.how: Wiring, cooling and transformers.

industries.name: Seat-based software
industries.how: If AI agents do the work, fewer human 'seats' are sold.

industries.name: The big spenders' cash flow
industries.how: Spending eats into free cash flow until it pays off.

active.breaks_if: Big tech cuts its spending plans, or AI revenue clearly fails to grow into the investment.
test: Copper price higher in three months
why_now: 4 recent headlines, e.g. "America’s $10tn AI infrastructure boom is starting to fray"

active.title: Big government deficits
active.first: The Treasury borrows more, selling more bonds.
active.second: To absorb all those bonds, investors demand higher long-term yields; mortgages and corporate borrowing follow them up. Spending itself boosts the industries it targets (defense, infrastructure, subsidised energy).
active.long_run: Interest on the debt grows into one of the largest budget items, crowding out other spending; worries about debt sustainability support gold and pressure the dollar.

industries.name: Defense & infrastructure
industries.how: Direct recipients of the spending.

industries.name: Gold
industries.how: A hedge against governments' debt problems.

industries.name: Long-term bonds
industries.how: More supply pushes their prices down, yields up.

industries.name: Housing
industries.how: Mortgage rates track the 10-year yield.

active.breaks_if: Growth outpaces the debt, or the Fed or foreign buyers absorb the bonds without needing higher yields.
test: 30-year Treasury yield higher in three months
why_now: 3 recent headlines, e.g. "U.S. budget deficit swells to almost $2 trillion for fiscal 2026, up 12% in a single year"

library.title: The Fed cuts rates
library.first: Short-term borrowing costs and savings rates fall.
library.second: Mortgage rates ease and housing activity picks up; floating-rate borrowers (small companies, private-equity-owned firms) get relief; the dollar tends to weaken, lifting US multinationals' overseas earnings.
library.long_run: Cheaper money encourages risk-taking - more IPOs, more speculation, more borrowing. If cuts come too early, inflation can return (the 1970s pattern).

industries.name: Homebuilders
industries.how: Lower mortgage rates bring buyers back.

industries.name: Small companies
industries.how: Most of their debt is floating-rate.

industries.name: Utilities & REITs
industries.how: Their dividends look better as bond yields fall.

industries.name: Emerging markets
industries.how: A weaker dollar eases their dollar debts.

industries.name: Money-market funds
industries.how: Yields fall straight away.

library.breaks_if: The Fed is cutting BECAUSE of a recession - then falling profits outweigh cheaper money for a while.
test: Mortgage rates lower in three months

library.title: Inflation won't come down
library.first: Prices keep rising faster than the Fed's 2% goal; wages chase them.
library.second: Companies that can raise prices without losing customers (strong brands, must-have software, monopolies) protect margins; companies that can't (low-margin retail, restaurants, contractors) get squeezed. The Fed holds rates high.
library.long_run: Expectations shift: workers demand bigger raises, companies raise prices pre-emptively - the hardest kind of inflation to stop, and the reason the Fed reacts strongly to early signs.

industries.name: Companies with pricing power
industries.how: Can pass costs on without losing customers.

industries.name: Commodity producers
industries.how: Their products ARE the rising prices.

industries.name: Inflation-protected bonds (TIPS)
industries.how: Payments rise with inflation.

industries.name: Low-margin retail & restaurants
industries.how: Costs rise faster than they can raise prices.

industries.name: Long-term bonds
industries.how: Fixed payments lose real value.

library.breaks_if: Rent and wage growth cool (they lag by months), or demand weakens enough to force discounting.
test: Two-year Treasury yield higher in two months

library.title: The job market weakens
library.first: Hiring slows, then layoffs rise; people feel less secure.
library.second: Spending on extras (travel, eating out, new cars) is cut first; credit-card and auto-loan losses rise at lenders; wage growth slows, which cools services inflation and lets the Fed cut.
library.long_run: Unemployment tends to rise in a self-reinforcing way once it starts - which is why the 'Sahm rule' (a 0.5-point rise) has called every recession since 1970.

industries.name: Discount retailers
industries.how: Shoppers trade down from pricier stores.

industries.name: Consumer staples & health care
industries.how: Spending on necessities barely moves.

industries.name: Staffing companies
industries.how: Temp hiring is the first thing cut.

industries.name: Card issuers & consumer lenders
industries.how: More borrowers fall behind.

industries.name: Travel, leisure & restaurants
industries.how: The first thing households trim.

library.breaks_if: Layoffs stay low - slower hiring without firing is a cooling, not a downturn.

library.title: Tariffs and trade barriers
library.first: Imported goods and parts cost more; trading partners often retaliate.
library.second: Importers and retailers choose between raising prices (inflation) and eating the cost (lower margins); manufacturers using imported parts (autos, machinery) pay more; exporters lose foreign sales to retaliation (farm products, aircraft).
library.long_run: Supply chains move - to Mexico, Vietnam, India, or back to the US. That takes years and builds factories, warehouses and automation, but leaves goods structurally more expensive.

industries.name: Domestic producers (steel, some manufacturing)
industries.how: Protected from cheaper imports.

industries.name: Factory construction & automation
industries.how: Firms build where the tariffs don't apply.

industries.name: Retailers & apparel
industries.how: Most goods are imported.

industries.name: Automakers
industries.how: Parts cross borders many times.

industries.name: Farm exporters & aerospace
industries.how: First targets of retaliation.

library.breaks_if: Deals or exemptions are announced, or tariffs are struck down in court.
test: Producer prices higher in three months

library.title: The dollar strengthens
library.first: US goods get more expensive abroad; imports get cheaper at home.
library.second: US multinationals earn less when foreign sales are converted back to dollars; countries and companies that borrowed in dollars find debts harder to repay; commodity prices (priced in dollars) tend to fall.
library.long_run: Persistent strength widens the trade deficit and draws political pressure (tariffs, calls for a weaker dollar).

industries.name: Importers & US travelers
industries.how: Foreign goods and trips get cheaper.

industries.name: Domestic-only small companies
industries.how: No currency hit to their sales.

industries.name: US multinationals
industries.how: Foreign profits shrink in dollar terms.

industries.name: Emerging markets
industries.how: Dollar debts get heavier.

industries.name: Commodities & gold
industries.how: Priced in dollars, so tend to fall.

library.breaks_if: US rates fall faster than other countries', removing the reason to hold dollars.

library.title: Borrowing gets harder
library.first: Lenders demand higher interest from riskier companies, or stop lending.
library.second: Weaker companies can't refinance and cut jobs and investment; private-equity-owned firms and private credit funds come under strain; banks tighten lending standards, slowing the whole economy.
library.long_run: A default cycle clears out weak firms over 1-2 years; survivors gain share. Credit has led stocks at most major turning points.

industries.name: Strong-balance-sheet companies
industries.how: Can buy weaker rivals cheaply.

industries.name: Government bonds
industries.how: Investors run to safety.

industries.name: High-debt companies
industries.how: Refinancing costs jump or money is unavailable.

industries.name: Private equity & private credit
industries.how: Their model depends on cheap borrowing.

industries.name: Regional banks
industries.how: Loan losses rise.

library.breaks_if: Spreads narrow again quickly - a scare, not a cycle.
test: Junk-bond spreads wider in two months

model.outlook: The data currently leans toward a soft landing, driven by cooling three-month inflation (2.05%) and low layoff claims (198.5k). However, high oil prices ($102/barrel) and rising 10-year Treasury yields (5.10%) threaten this path by keeping overall borrowing costs elevated. A sustained spike in producer prices or persistent sticky inflation would quickly push the market toward a higher-rate or stagflationary environment.

soft_landing.from_here: As inflation continues to cool toward target levels, the Federal Reserve can gradually ease interest rates without crashing the labor market. Moderate job growth and stable consumer spending would allow company earnings to grow steadily over the long term.
soft_landing.tipping_point: Monthly job growth rising back above 75,000 alongside a stable 3-month core inflation reading below 2.5%.

running_hot.from_here: Surging energy prices from global disruptions will trickle down into broader consumer goods, reigniting inflation pressure. In response, the Fed will be forced to raise interest rates further, increasing borrowing costs across the economy.
running_hot.tipping_point: Core inflation on a 3-month basis climbing back above 3.0% combined with sustained monthly oil prices over $100.

stagflation.from_here: High energy prices will act like a tax on businesses and consumers, dragging down economic growth while keeping overall inflation stubbornly elevated. Companies will face rising operational costs even as consumer demand weakens, shrinking profit margins.
stagflation.tipping_point: The unemployment rate climbing past 4.5% while energy-driven inflation remains stuck above 3.0%.

downturn.from_here: High long-term interest rates will severely restrict business spending and hiring, causing slow monthly job additions (29k) to turn into widespread job cuts. Declining consumer demand would then force rapid price cuts and trigger central bank rate cuts to revive activity.
downturn.tipping_point: Weekly layoff claims rising consistently above 260,000 while monthly payroll gains turn negative.

chains.event: US budget deficit swells to almost $2 trillion
chains.first: The US government must sell a massive volume of Treasury bonds to fund its shortfalls, forcing bond yields higher to attract buyers.
chains.second: Higher yields on government debt elevate mortgage rates, corporate loan rates, and borrowing costs for technology infrastructure.
chains.long_run: Over several years, heavy government debt service crowds out private investment, forcing corporate tax revisions or prolonged elevated benchmark rates.
